title: Priests, Levites, and the LORD as Their Portion
summary: God speaks directly to Aaron, assigning the priests responsibility for guarding the sanctuary and the altar and giving the Levites to assist them, so that wrath will not fall on Israel again. He grants the priests a share of the offerings, firstfruits, devoted things, and firstborn, and gives the Levites the tithes of Israel in place of land. The Levites in turn must give a tenth of their tithe, the best part, to the priests.
story: Chapter 17 ended with the people crying that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die. Chapter 18 is God's answer. It is unusual in that God speaks directly to Aaron (verses 1, 8, and 20), which happens rarely in the Pentateuch. After the rebellion of Korah and the plague, God does not remove his presence from the camp; he sets up a protected structure around it. The priests and Levites will stand guard and bear the risk, and the people will be able to live near God without being consumed. The chapter also settles how the priests and Levites will live, since they will receive no territory when Israel enters the land. Chapter 19 will then provide a way to cleanse the people from the impurity of death, which the recent plague had brought on a massive scale.
historical:
The law is set in the wilderness, but it looks ahead to Israel's settled life in Canaan, where the other tribes would receive land and the Levites would not. Later books show this arrangement in practice: Joshua 21 assigns the Levites towns with pasturelands scattered among the tribes rather than a single territory, and Nehemiah 10 and 13 show the returned exiles recommitting to bring the tithes to the Levites and the Levites' tithe to the priests, and the trouble that followed when they didn't.

The redemption price for a firstborn son was five shekels of silver by the sanctuary shekel (verse 16). A shekel was a unit of weight rather than a coin in this period, commonly estimated at somewhere around 11 or 12 grams, though estimates vary, and the sanctuary shekel was a fixed standard of twenty gerahs. Five shekels was a real but manageable sum, the same amount set for redeeming the firstborn in Numbers 3:47.
cultural:
Israel's economy was agricultural, so the gifts are counted in grain, new wine, olive oil, and livestock. The firstfruits were the first and best of each harvest, brought to God as an acknowledgment that the whole harvest was his. The firstborn of people and animals were also claimed by God, because he had spared Israel's firstborn when he struck Egypt's (Exodus 13). Firstborn sons and unclean animals like donkeys were redeemed with a payment, while firstborn cattle, sheep, and goats were sacrificed and their meat went to the priests. Devoted things (verse 14) were items set apart wholly to God, which could not be sold or redeemed.

A tithe is a tenth. Israel's tithe went to the Levites as their wages for serving at the Tent of Meeting, and the Levites passed on a tenth of that, the best of it, to the priests. Deuteronomy 14 describes further uses of the tithe, including a festival meal and provision for the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow in the third year; how these tithing laws fit together was a question later Jewish interpreters worked out in detail. The covenant of salt (verse 19) was an image of permanence: salt preserves and does not decay, and the same phrase is used of God's covenant with David's house (2 Chronicles 13:5).
literary: The chapter is built from three divine speeches to Aaron (verses 1 to 7, 8 to 19, and 20 to 24) and one to Moses for the Levites (25 to 32). The first speech is about duty and danger, the second about the priests' income, the third about the Levites' income, and the last about the Levites' own giving. Recurring phrases tie it together: bear the iniquity, attend to the duties (literally guard the charge), come near, and die. The word gift is striking in verses 6 and 7, where God calls both the Levites and the priesthood itself a gift. The central line of the chapter is verse 20: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites.”

outline.t: The duties of priests and Levites in guarding the sanctuary
The priests' share of offerings, firstfruits, and firstborn
No land for Levi: the tithe as inheritance
The Levites' tithe of the tithe

doctrines.note: God's holiness remains dangerous, but he places guardians around it so that his presence can bless rather than destroy. The priests and Levites stand in the gap so that “wrath may not fall on the Israelites again” (verse 5).

The priests' share is called a permanent statute and a “permanent covenant of salt” (verse 19). God binds himself to provide for those who serve him, and the arrangement is rooted in his faithfulness rather than their merit.
Firstfruits, firstborn, and tithes teach that all of life belongs to God. Giving the first and best part acknowledges him as the giver of the whole.

words.note: Nachalah, inheritance, especially land passed down within a family and tribe. For every other tribe it meant a share of Canaan. For Aaron and the Levites it is redefined: God himself is their inheritance, and the tithe is how that is made concrete.

Ma'aser, tithe, a tenth. The word first appears for Abraham's gift to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:20) and Jacob's vow (Genesis 28:22). Here it becomes the Levites' permanent support, and even the Levites must give a tithe of what they receive.

Mishmeret, charge, duty, or guard. The BSB renders it with the verb attend to the duties, but the word often carries the sense of guard duty. The Levites and priests are sentries around the holy place, protecting the people as much as the sanctuary.

Mattanah, gift. God calls the Levites a gift to the priests (verse 6) and the priesthood a gift to Aaron (verse 7). After Korah treated the priesthood as a prize to be seized, the chapter insists it is something given.

christ: The chapter is part of the priestly system that the New Testament says finds its fulfillment in Christ. Hebrews argues that the Levitical priests served a copy of the heavenly sanctuary and that Jesus, a priest of a different order, entered God's presence once for all (Hebrews 7 to 9). The fear of approaching God that runs through Numbers 17 and 18 is answered in the gospel by a mediator who opens the way (Hebrews 10:19-22). Peter calls the church a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), extending priestly access to all God's people in a way Korah had wrongly claimed for himself and that only Christ's work makes possible. The promise that the LORD is Aaron's portion is echoed in the psalms of individual believers, who call God their portion (Psalm 16:5; 73:26). Paul also draws on this chapter's logic when he argues that those who serve at the altar share in its offerings and that those who proclaim the gospel should live by it (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

hard.q: Does this chapter mean Christians are required to tithe?
hard.a:
Christians answer this in several ways. Some hold that the tithe is an abiding standard: they note that Abraham gave a tenth before the law of Moses (Genesis 14:20), that Jesus mentions tithing without abolishing it (Matthew 23:23), and that Paul applies the principle of supporting those who serve at the altar to ministers of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:13-14). Others argue that the tithe was part of the Mosaic system tied to the Levitical priesthood, the land, and the temple, all of which are fulfilled in Christ, and that the New Testament never commands a tenth but calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate giving (2 Corinthians 8 and 9). Many in this second group still regard a tenth as a wise starting point rather than a rule.

The chapter's own concern is clear on either reading. God's people are to support those who serve in his worship, to give the best rather than the leftovers, and to recognize that everything they have belongs to God. Even the Levites, who lived on gifts, were required to give.

questions: The Levites received no land and were told that God was their inheritance. What would it mean for you to treat God himself as your portion rather than only as the giver of portions?
Even the Levites, who lived on the tithes of others, had to give the best tenth of what they received. How does giving from the best change the way you hold what you have?
God calls the priesthood and the Levites gifts. How might it change your view of service in your church to see it as a gift rather than a status or a burden?
